metadata.topic: WHAT IS GRU? — E2/6: THE FIVE SUPERVISORY CAPACITIES

beats.narration_text: Ciao — this is Liam. Episode 2 of 6. In Episode 1 we established the conductor metaphor — you specify, Claude executes, the gap between meant and understood is where the damage lives. This episode is about the five labels Gru uses to mark the human side of that gap. Learn these five and you can read any Boondoggle Score. Miss them and the score is just formatting. Five minutes. Let's go.

props.topic: WHAT IS GRU? — E2/6: THE FIVE SUPERVISORY CAPACITIES
props.segment: The Five Supervisory Capacities: What Only You Can Do
props.command: Open your Gru session. Run /claude on any in-progress SDD and locate the supervisory-capacity labels on the GRU steps.
props.runningText: five labels — every human step in the score carries one — they are the irreducibly human parts…
output: Score returned — GRU steps each carry a capacity label: [PA], [PF], [TO], [IJ], [EI]
Distribution summary visible — any capacity at zero is flagged

beats.narration_text: The Boondoggle Score divides every step of your build into two columns. The MINION column is Claude's side — tasks where the specification is complete enough that Claude can execute without making irreducibly human decisions. The GRU column is your side — steps that require judgment Claude cannot supply. Every step in the GRU column carries one of five capacity labels. These labels are not bureaucratic jargon. They are the taxonomy of what 'irreducibly human' actually means in a software build. The five are: PA for Plausibility Auditing, PF for Problem Formulation, TO for Tool Orchestration, IJ for Interpretive Judgment, and EI for Executive Integration. Each names a specific kind of judgment that requires domain knowledge, accountability, or the ability to hold multiple things in tension — none of which Claude can supply. If any capacity appears zero times in a score, Gru flags it. A build with no Plausibility Auditing steps, for example, assumes Claude is always right. That is a boondoggle.

lines: Every GRU step in the score carries one of these five labels
[PA] Plausibility Auditing — hearing the wrong note before verification

beats.narration_text: Plausibility Auditing — PA — is the capacity to hear the wrong note before you have verified it. A trained musician knows a note is off before they check the sheet music. A domain expert knows an output is wrong before they run the test suite. PA is that pre-verification sense of 'this doesn't sound right.' Claude cannot do this because plausibility requires domain grounding. Claude generates outputs that are internally consistent; it cannot detect outputs that are externally wrong against a domain it doesn't inhabit. Every step in the score that says 'review this output for face validity' or 'check that the logic matches what you know about the domain' is a PA step. Problem Formulation — PF — is earlier and harder. It is the capacity to decide what the mission is before Claude sees any of it. The /v0 gate is a PF gate — it will not proceed until you can name the thing being built in one sentence. If you cannot formulate the problem, Claude will formulate it for you — and the mission you specified is whatever Claude inferred from your vague input. PF steps in the score are the ones that cannot be delegated because they determine the shape of everything that follows.

lines: [PA] Hearing the wrong note before verification
Claude produces internally consistent outputs. Only you can detect externally wrong ones.

beats.narration_text: Tool Orchestration — TO — is the capacity to decide which Claude task runs, in what order, with what level of trust. This is the conductor's role in the literal sense: you are sequencing the instruments. TO steps are not individual Claude prompts. They are decisions about the dependency structure of the build — which outputs gate which inputs, which tasks can run in parallel, which tasks require human review before the next task starts. Claude can suggest a sequence. Only you can authorize it, because only you know what failure in one step would cost the steps downstream. Interpretive Judgment — IJ — is the capacity to supply meaning and accountability that Claude cannot. When an output is technically correct but domain-wrong — when the model follows the spec precisely but the spec was missing a constraint you forgot to write — IJ is the capacity that catches it. IJ steps are where you read the output not just for correctness against the spec but for validity against the world. These are often the hardest steps to identify because they look like review steps. The difference is that IJ review cannot be done by running more tests. It requires a human who knows what the system is supposed to mean.

lines: [TO] Which Claude task, in what order, with what trust
TO decisions: dependency structure , parallel vs. sequential , what gates what.

beats.act: EI in depth + reading the score
beats.narration_text: Executive Integration — EI — is the capacity that holds the other four together toward one coherent goal. It is the highest-level and least-visible capacity because it operates across the whole build, not at individual steps. EI is what you exercise when you notice that the outputs of two Claude tasks are technically correct individually but contradictory in combination — when a component passes its own tests but breaks a constraint set by a component three steps earlier. EI steps in the score are often the last step before a handoff — the step where you decide whether the integrated whole is ready to proceed. Now, how to read the score. The GRU column lists your steps in dependency order. Each step names the capacity label, the action, and the handoff condition — the testable check that determines whether the next step can start. When you look at the distribution summary at the bottom of the score, you are looking for two things: any capacity at zero, which Gru will flag, and any cluster of steps — three or more of the same capacity in a row — which often means a part of the build that is underspecified and will require more human judgment than the score currently shows.

lines: [EI] Holds all four capacities toward one coherent goal
EI catches two correct outputs that contradict each other in combination.

beats.narration_text: Verdict for The Five Supervisory Capacities. Every human step in the Boondoggle Score carries one of five labels. PA — Plausibility Auditing: hear it before you prove it. PF — Problem Formulation: decide the mission before Claude sees it. TO — Tool Orchestration: you sequence, you authorize. IJ — Interpretive Judgment: technically correct but domain-wrong? That's yours. EI — Executive Integration: two outputs contradict each other in combination? That's yours too. When reading a score, check the distribution: any capacity at zero is a boondoggle assumption. Three or more of the same label in a row is an underspecified zone. These five labels are not a taxonomy for a grade. They are a map of where the damage will come from if you skip the step.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Think of a build you know — something you have built with Claude or plan to build. It does not need to be your Boondoggle app. It can be anything you worked on where Claude was involved. Now name one moment in that build that needed each of the five capacities. One PA moment: when did you look at Claude's output and think 'something is off' before you could prove it? One PF moment: when did you decide what the task actually was, before Claude could? One TO moment: when did you decide the order two Claude tasks needed to run? One IJ moment: when was the output technically correct but wrong for the domain? One EI moment: when did two pieces of the build contradict each other? Write the five in a list. The capacities you cannot name are your blind spots — they are the steps you were skipping without noticing. That list is your starting profile for reading the Boondoggle Score.
